evals.prompt: Can you rewrite my title and abstract so it reads like the highly cited papers in Lancet Global Health? I want it to get noticed and cited. Draft: evals/files/draft_title_abstract.md
evals.expected_output: A new title stating topic, population, scale and period, and a structured Lancet-style abstract (Background, Methods, Findings, Interpretation, Funding) that keeps every number exactly, leads Findings with the headline estimate and CI, replaces the generic gap and overclaiming conclusion, and adds placeholders for missing facts (funding, survey years where needed).
expectations: No em dashes, en dashes or double hyphens
No prose sentence of 30 or more words
All numbers from the draft are preserved exactly
No new numbers are introduced that are not in the draft
Title names the countries or region, the scale (7 countries or 38,412 adults) and the period
Title does not inflate scope (no 'global' or 'worldwide')
Uses Lancet headings: Background, Methods, Findings, Interpretation, Funding
Findings open with the headline estimate and its 95% CI (27.4%, 26.6 to 28.2)
Interpretation drops the 'governments must take urgent action' mandate and names an action the data support
Vague gap ('few studies') replaced with a specific gap or placeholder
Funding left as a placeholder rather than invented

evals.prompt: I have these results on stunting trends by wealth across 30 African countries (evals/files/stunting_results_summary.md). Which figures should I make for Lancet Global Health, what should each one show, and can you give me captions and R code to start from?
evals.expected_output: A figure plan in which the first figure carries the headline finding, using trend lines with uncertainty, a ranked country chart or map, and an inequality chart (equiplot or SII), with stand-alone captions and adaptable ggplot2 code, using only the user's numbers.
expectations: No em dashes, en dashes or double hyphens
No prose sentence of 30 or more words (outside code)
Figure 1 shows the headline finding (pooled stunting decline 41.6% to 32.1%)
Includes a trend figure with uncertainty shown
Includes a country-level figure of annual change (ranked chart or map)
Includes a wealth inequality figure (quintiles, equiplot or slope index)
Captions state measure, population, place, years and what intervals show
Provides R ggplot2 code
Uses only the user's numbers (no invented country values)
Handles the ambiguous Zambia note consistently (decline of -0.9) or flags it

evals.prompt: I'm planning a paper on hypertension care cascades using WHO STEPS surveys from 12 South and Southeast Asian countries. Honestly, what makes public health papers get cited a lot, and how should I design and write mine so it has the best chance? Be specific.
evals.expected_output: Evidence-based advice tied to the top-100 analysis: contribution types that earn citations (reusable estimates, methods, frameworks), concrete design and writing choices (quotable uncertainty-bounded numbers, scale in title, shareable estimates and code, figures), honest caveats about what cannot be copied and correlation versus cause, without inventing statistics.
expectations: No em dashes, en dashes or double hyphens
No prose sentence of 30 or more words
Explains that most highly cited papers supply reusable outputs (estimates, methods, standards, frameworks)
Gives study-specific design advice (cascade estimates with intervals by country, sex or age; standard definitions)
Recommends sharing estimates, code or data
Advises a title stating scope, scale and period
Advises a quotable headline number with its uncertainty
Recommends specific figure types (map, trends, cascade chart)
States honest caveats (journal, consortium or timing cannot be copied; association not cause)
Warns against citation gaming or overclaiming
Makes no unsupported quantitative claims about citation effects
